Would it be possible to set up a macOS x86 runner for pre-merge checks?  That would 1) allow us to catch macOS build problems before merging and 2) distinguish between "the pipeline failed because of a problem with building and testing on macOS" (whether it's a problem with the code on macOS or with the way the macOS runners are set up) and "the pipeline failed because of a problem with building and testing on macOS *on ARM*".
That should be possible. But we should not allow running arbitrary code on the machine...

Done in the latest commit, but the first ninja step is failing. Is the binary x64-only?

> Done in the latest commit, but the first ninja step is failing. Is the binary x64-only?

For ninja v1.10.2, if I download ninja-mac.zip and extract ninja from it, I get:

```
$ ninja
ninja: Mach-O universal binary with 2 architectures: [x86_64:Mach-O 64-bit executable x86_64] [arm64:Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64]
ninja (for architecture x86_64):	Mach-O 64-bit executable x86_64
ninja (for architecture arm64):	Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64
```

so the answer for the latest version is "no".

Currently, macos-setup.sh downloads version 1.8.2, for which file reports:

```
ninja: Mach-O 64-bit executable x86_64
```

I infer from [this Google Groups message](https://groups.google.com/g/ninja-build/c/oobwq_F0PpA/m/FeJC5LoRBgAJ) that 1.10.2 is the first x86/ARM fat binary release for Ninja.

Unless somebody knows a reason why macos-setup.sh should *not* immediately be updated to install Ninja 1.10.2, I vote we do that.

> We might want to add `arch -arch arm64` to commands which are computational expensive. Currently, for example, all compilation is done with an intel clang using emulation. Running it natively will be faster.

If you're running on an ARM machine:

- If XXX is an x86-64/ARM64 fat binary, shouldn't the results of `arch -arch arm64 XXX` be the same as the results of `XXX`?  Or are we somehow forcing the default to x86-64, so that even if ARM64 code is available, it won't be run?
- If XXX is an x86-64-only binary, `arch -arch arm64 XXX` won't magically make it run native, it'll fail; the one useful thing it *does* do is point out when we *don't* have fat binaries, so we can look at updating them if fat binaries are available.

I would vote for updating ninja.

The reason for using `arch -arch arm64` is not that I expect the result to be different, but that the build process is faster, since it is running a native binary instead of the x86_64 on. I think this is a consequence of `gitlab-runner` being a x86_64 only binary right now.
No objection here, although something like `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /path/to/ninja` might be required: https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/issues/1695

How is this broken?  Let me count the ways....

1. Why is it wasting time looking up anything about capture devices when it's been told do just dump out all the registered fields?  (Generic problem, not macOS-specific, much less macOS-on-ARM64-specific.)
1. Why would there be *two* instances of TShark?  During the time between the fork and the exec, OK, but once the exec is done, it should be showing the extcap program.  Is the fork just taking Too Damn Long?

I'll have to look at `g_spawn_sync()`, but we might be better off doing our own version, which could use `posix_spawn()` if available - at least on macOS, where it was added to, among other things, get rid of various fork overheads on macOS - `fork()` and `exec()` if it's a UN\*X and not available, and `CreateProcess()` on Windows.

(In the past few weeks, I saw some other run-a-program case in Wireshark which looked like another case where using `posix_spawn()` on macOS might speed things up, as it was doing a bunch of random crap as part of forking.)
BTW: running `tshark -D` or `wireshark -D` shows the same symptom. Actually starting `wireshark` with a GUI seems to work fine.

Reproduced on an x86-64 Big Sur virtual machine with `tshark --version`!

Probably not ARM-related.
Yepp, I can reproduce it as well on ARM...

On the VM where TShark is currently stuck, the processes for the terminal in which I ran TShark are:

$ ps -ft s000

So process 419 is my shell, 595 is the TShark that I ran, and 597 and 598 are both extcap subprocesses, with 597 being an androiddump that's finished (the parentheses indicate a zombie process, for which only the executable image name is available) and 598 is stuck trying to get to the point where it executes whatever extcap program it's supposed to run.

> Why the global lock appears to be held is a good question.

Perhaps it *is* held, because, at the instant the `fork()` took effect, it was held by another thread in the parent, and that got copied over into the child, as per the "Known issues" section in [the README for the KIT-IBPT/epics-execute repository](https://github.com/KIT-IBPT/epics-execute/blob/master/README.md):

> On macOS (at least on macOS 10.12), it can happen that the execution of a command is started, but the actual executable is never invoked and the forked process is stalled indefinitely.
> 
> This problem is caused by a bug in the loader (dyld): When using fork() in a multi-threaded program, it can happen that the loader tries to acquire a mutex in the forked process that had been held by another thread in the process that called fork(). This happens even when only using async signal safe functions in the forked process. Whenn inspecting the forked process in the debugger, the stack trace looks like this:
> 
> ```
> frame #0: 0x00007fffe14a8c22 libsystem_kernel.dylib`__psynch_mutexwait + 10
> frame #1: 0x00007fffe1593dfa libsystem_pthread.dylib`_pthread_mutex_lock_wait + 100
> frame #2: 0x00007fffe1591519 libsystem_pthread.dylib`_pthread_mutex_lock_slow + 285
> frame #3: 0x00007fffe1376118 libdyld.dylib`dyldGlobalLockAcquire() + 16
> frame #4: 0x0000000115ce4f96 dyld`ImageLoaderMachOCompressed::doBindFastLazySymbol(unsigned int, ImageLoader::LinkContext const&, void (*)(), void (*)()) + 54
> frame #5: 0x0000000115ccc86d dyld`dyld::fastBindLazySymbol(ImageLoader**, unsigned long) + 90
> frame #6: 0x00007fffe1376282 libdyld.dylib`dyld_stub_binder + 282
> frame #7: 0x0000000109cb6320 libexecute.dylib
> ```
> 
> Unfortunately, there is no workaround for this bug that can be implemented in the code. The only known workaround is disabling lazy binding when linking the device support library. This can be achieved by adding the following line to configure/CONFIG_SITE.local:
> 
> ```
> USR_LDFLAGS += -bind_at_load
> ```

`fork()` + pthreads = [potential issues on Linux as well](https://www.linuxprogrammingblog.com/threads-and-fork-think-twice-before-using-them), [and again](https://lwn.net/Articles/674712/).  The same applies for every other UN\*X with pthreads.

I'm not sure why the GLib configure script thinks `posix_spawn()` isn't available on macOS; I'll look at the configure script and config.log.

To quote a comment in the `g_spawn_sync()` code:

```
 * On modern UNIX platforms, GLib can use an efficient process launching
 * codepath driven internally by posix_spawn(). This has the advantage of
 * avoiding the fork-time performance costs of cloning the parent process
 * address space, and avoiding associated memory overcommit checks that are
 * not relevant in the context of immediately executing a distinct process.
 * This optimized codepath will be used provided that the following conditions
 * are met:
 *
 * 1. %G_SPAWN_DO_NOT_REAP_CHILD is set
 * 2. %G_SPAWN_LEAVE_DESCRIPTORS_OPEN is set
 * 3. %G_SPAWN_SEARCH_PATH_FROM_ENVP is not set
 * 4. @working_directory is %NULL
 * 5. @child_setup is %NULL
 * 6. The program is of a recognised binary format, or has a shebang. Otherwise, GLib will have to execute the program through the shell, which is not done using the optimized codepath.
```

In `ws_pipe_spawn_sync()`, `working_directory` is non-null if it's non-null in the `ws_pipe_spawn_sync()` call, and we're not setting `G_SPAWN_DO_NOT_REAP_CHILD` and we're only setting `G_SPAWN_LEAVE_DESCRIPTORS_OPEN` on Linux as a bug workaround.

We should address this if we can.  (Dear GLib maintainers: `posix_spawn()` also avoids the hell of locked mutexes remaining locked in the child after a `fork()`, and note that those mutexes might belong to *OS code* over which you and the application don't have control....)

At least on macOS, there's a `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` flag that can be set with `posix_spawnattr_setflags()`:

     POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT  Apple Extension: If this bit is set, then
                                  only file descriptors explicitly created by
                                  the file_actions argument are available in
                                  the spawned process; all of the other file
                                  descriptors are automatically closed in the
                                  spawned process.

and there's a file action "inherit" that can be set with `posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np()` to indicate that a particular FD should be inherited by the child process.

(On Windows, `CreateProcess()` on Windows will cause the child process not to inherit any of the parent's handles if the `bInheritHandles` parameter is FALSE; you can then pass the standard input/output/error handles to the child, but have nothing else available.  We pass TRUE in the pipe-spawning code, but maybe we shouldn't....)

That's a way, on macOS, to close all the extra FDs without having `g_spawn_sync()` do it and without having to set `FD_CLOEXEC` on a pile of FDs.

As for `G_SPAWN_DO_NOT_REAP_CHILD`, yeah, if we use `posix_spawn()` we'll have to do a `waitpid()`, but we're already doing the equivalent on Windows.

We're already not using `child_setup` on anything other than Linux, so that's not an issue.

That leaves the working directory; on macOS, we have `posix_spawn_file_actions_addchdir_np()`, which adds a `chdir()` to the file operations performed by `posix_spawn()`.  `_np` stands for "not portable" or "not POSIX", but if we just do this for macOS, that's not a problem - if we have fork + pthreads = 🤢 on any other platform, we can see if we can address it using various features for that platform.

According to [the Development/LifeCycle Wiki page](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/wikis/Development/LifeCycle), we don't support any version of NeXTSTEP-ng :-) prior to 10.12 (i.e., if the OS isn't named "macOS", you lose :-))

`POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` and `posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np()` date back to 10.7, if the current spawn.h is to be believed, so it's available in 10.12 and later (I checked the man page, it is).

Sadly, `posix_spawn_file_actions_addchdir_np()` was introduced in Catalina, so we can't use all those tricks except in Catalina and later. ([It may have been a Solaris invention](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E88353_01/html/E37843/posix-spawn-file-actions-addchdir-np-3c.html); [it was proposed for POSIX in September 2018](https://www.austingroupbugs.net/view.php?id=1208), but it's not in POSIX yet.

So we shouldn't have to do anything special to use `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` and `posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np()` on macOS, other than having `#ifdef __APPLE__`.

For `posix_spawn_file_actions_addchdir_np()`, however, we'd have to either 1) find it with `dlopen()` and `dlsym()` or 2) build with a 10.15 or later SDK and only use `posix_spawn()` if `posix_spawn_file_actions_addchdir_np != NULL`.  (Yes, seriously, it *can* evaluate to a null pointer!  See [Apple's page on "Frameworks and Weak Linking"](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/MacOSX/Conceptual/BPFrameworks/Concepts/WeakLinking.html) - it says "frameworks", but it also applies to Boring Old Shared Libraries.

(`posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np()` is, unfortunately, available neither on tvOS nor watchOS, so we'll run the risk of hanging on startup with extcaps if you're trying to use your TV or your watch as a sniffer. :-))

(The history of `posix_spawn()` is a bit interesting; it apparently was initially created to make POSIX process spawning on MMUless systems less painful, by not requiring `fork()`.  I guess it's also being used to simplify spawning processes in multithreaded programs etc., which may be why all this other stuff is being added.)

Possibly, but that's elsewhere.

At least part of the problem is due to calling `signal()`, but that's because everybody with a clue (including Wireshark) is calling `sigaction()`, not `signal()`, for anything that involves setting a signal action.  If code running after a `fork()` is the first code in either the parent or the child to call `signal()`, that means that the run-time linker is called to resolve it (a call to a function that's already been called wouldn't need that).  If, at the time of the fork, some other thread was resolving something and held the global run-time linker lock, the child process's address space would have that lock held, and the run-time linker in the child tries to get that lock and hangs forever.

(The history of `signal()` vs. `sigaction()`: in some UN\*Xes, `signal()` still has its traditional Bell Labs semantics, wherein, when a signal is delivered, the handler is reset to `SIG_DFL`, so that if another such signal arrives before the handler is set again, the program will probably be terminated by the signal.  4.2BSD changed that to, instead, add the signal to the signal mask (the equivalent of an interrupt setting the interrupt level/mask so that the interrupt in question is masked so that it's not delivered until it's unmasked), but that's an incompatible change.

Setting the action to `SIG_DFL` or `SIG_IGN` with `signal()` is safe, because there is no handler, but it's probably best to get out of the habit of using `signal()` at all.)
